title: Judges 4:17–24
context: The closing verses of the chapter follow Sisera on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, whose household was at peace with Jabin. Jael welcomes him, gives him milk, covers him, and while he sleeps drives a tent peg through his temple. When Barak arrives, she shows him the dead commander, fulfilling Deborah’s word that the LORD would sell Sisera into a woman’s hand. The chapter ends by crediting the victory to God, who subdued Jabin before Israel. This passage deserves moral seriousness. Jael’s act involves hospitality turned into deadly deception, and the narrator reports it without commentary, while the Song in chapter 5 later praises her. Both traditions affirm that God’s purposes were accomplished in this deliverance, and both recognize that the text raises real ethical questions about the means, questions readers should hold honestly rather than resolve too quickly.

verses.text: However Sisera fled away on his feet to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite; for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, because Heber’s house was at peace with Jabin. He seeks safety with those he considers allies.

Arminian readers note that Heber’s household had made its own alliances, and Sisera trusts that arrangement. Jael’s response will show that she chose a different allegiance, a decision that carries great weight in the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s providence bringing Sisera to the very place where Deborah’s prophecy will be fulfilled. The commander who fled the battlefield cannot escape the hand of the LORD.

Both traditions agree that the peace between Jabin and Heber’s house is central to the moral seriousness of what follows, since Jael acts against a political arrangement as well as against a fleeing guest.

verses.text: Jael went out to meet Sisera, and said to him, “Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; don’t be afraid.” He came in to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jael goes out to meet Sisera, invites him to turn aside to her and not be afraid, and covers him with a rug once he enters the tent. Her welcome appears to offer him safety.

Arminian readers note that Jael’s words reassure Sisera, though her later action shows they were not what they seemed. The text invites readers to weigh honestly the use of deception and hospitality in this moment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the narrator reports Jael’s welcome without commentary, leaving her motives unstated. Whether she planned from the beginning or decided later is not clear from the text.

Both traditions agree that ancient expectations of hospitality made this welcome weighty, and that the story asks readers to take seriously the tension between Jael’s hospitality and her deadly act.

verses.text: He said to her, “Please give me a little water to drink; for I am thirsty.” She opened a container of milk, and gave him a drink, and covered him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sisera asks for a little water, and Jael opens a container of milk, gives him a drink, and covers him again. She gives more than he asks.

Arminian readers note that Jael’s generosity deepens Sisera’s trust. The details show a man exhausted and dependent, and the scene presses readers to consider the moral weight of what she will do to someone who has placed himself in her care.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the narrator slows down the scene with domestic detail, drawing attention to the ordinary acts that precede the decisive one. God’s purpose is accomplished through an unexpected person in an unexpected setting.

Both traditions agree that the verse should be read soberly, as a careful narrative detail rather than a scene of humor, preparing for the solemn climax of the chapter.

verses.text: He said to her, “Stand in the door of the tent, and if any man comes and inquires of you, and says, ‘Is there any man here?’ you shall say, ‘No.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Sisera asks Jael to stand in the tent door and deny that anyone is inside if asked. He depends completely on her protection.

Arminian readers note that Sisera asks Jael to lie for him. The scene is full of deception on more than one side, and readers should recognize the moral complexity of a world in which survival and loyalty are tangled together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe the irony that the commander of nine hundred chariots now relies on a woman at a tent door, fulfilling Deborah’s word that the LORD would sell Sisera into a woman’s hand.

Both traditions agree that the verse reveals Sisera’s helplessness after the defeat and prepares for Jael’s decisive act, without making that act morally simple or easy to evaluate.

verses.text: Then Jael, Heber’s wife, took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand, and went softly to him, and struck the pin into his temples, and it pierced through into the ground, for he was in a deep sleep; so he fainted and died.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jael takes a tent peg and a hammer, goes quietly to Sisera while he sleeps deeply, and drives the peg through his temple into the ground, and he dies. The act is reported with stark directness.

Arminian readers take seriously the gravity of this killing. It ends the oppressor’s life and the oppression of Israel, but it also violates the hospitality Jael had offered, and the text does not hide that tension.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator presents Jael’s act as the means of fulfilling God’s word, and the Song in chapter 5 blesses her (Judges 5:24). Yet God’s use of an act does not make every aspect of it a model for imitation.

Both traditions agree that the verse should be read with moral seriousness, recognizing God’s judgment on Sisera while honestly acknowledging the ethical questions the means raise.

verses.text: Behold, as Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him, and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man whom you seek.” He came to her; and behold, Sisera lay dead, and the tent peg was in his temples.
verses.arminianNotes:
As Barak pursues Sisera, Jael comes out and offers to show him the man he is seeking. Barak enters and finds Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple.

Arminian readers note that Barak arrives too late to capture Sisera himself, just as Deborah said. His earlier hesitation has shaped the outcome, and the honor of ending Sisera’s life belongs to Jael.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the precise fulfillment of Deborah’s prophecy that the LORD would sell Sisera into a woman’s hand. God’s word comes true in a way no one in the story could have anticipated at the start.

Both traditions agree that the verse brings the story of Sisera to its end and confirms that God’s word through his prophet is trustworthy, even when it is fulfilled in surprising ways.

verses.text: So God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel on that day.
verses.arminianNotes:
So God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before Israel that day. The narrator steps back from Barak and Jael to name the true agent of the victory.

Arminian readers note that, for all the human actions in the story, the narrator credits God with the outcome. The people’s faith and obedience mattered, but the deliverance is ultimately God’s gracious answer to their cry.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that this verse summarizes the whole chapter: God subdued Jabin. Deborah, Barak, the tribes, and Jael are all instruments of a victory that belongs to God alone.

Both traditions agree that the verse is the theological key to the passage, placing the human drama of the battle and Jael’s tent within the larger story of God’s faithfulness to his covenant people.

verses.text: The hand of the children of Israel prevailed more and more against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
verses.arminianNotes:
The hand of Israel prevails more and more against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroy him. The victory at the Kishon becomes the beginning of a sustained campaign.

Arminian readers note that Israel continues to act on the victory God has given, pressing on until the oppression is ended completely. Deliverance opens the way, but the people must keep walking in it faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the gradual increase of Israel’s strength the steady outworking of God’s purpose. What began with a decisive act of God continues until the oppressor is fully removed.

Both traditions agree that the chapter closes with the end of Jabin’s rule, and that the Song of Deborah in chapter 5 will retell the victory in poetry and give praise to the LORD for it.
